questions.stem: Sluysmans and Colan proposed that the optimal size of a cardiovascular structure minimizes the hemodynamic cost of providing blood flow. According to this **principle of minimal work**, the optimal radius of a valve or vessel is the radius that:

choices.text: Stays the same whatever the cardiac output
Minimizes viscous energy loss alone, which falls as the radius increases
Minimizes the inertial energy content of blood alone
Minimizes the sum of viscous energy loss and inertial energy content
Is calculated for the resting cardiac output only

explanation.text: The optimal radius sits at the **minimum of the total energy loss curve**: the sum of **viscous energy loss** and **inertial energy content**.

explanation.title: Two energies pull in opposite directions

steps.text: Radius of valve or vessel

branches.label: viscous
branches.text: Shear stress is related to **inverse** radius -> larger radius, less viscous loss

branches.label: inertial
branches.text: Inertial energy (pulsatile flow) is **directly** related to radius

steps.label: sum
steps.text: Lowest total energy loss = ==optimal radius==

explanation.caption: Fig. 1.32: optimal aortic valve radius, normal subject with BSA 1 m²
head: Theoretical cardiac output
Represents
Optimal radius

explanation.text: These two values are the **theoretical range of normal** optimal aortic valve radius for this BSA: normal pathways carry flow at rest **and** during exercise and stress with little or no pressure drop.
To achieve minimum work requires minimizing viscous energy (shear stress related to inverse vessel radius) and inertial energy related to pulsatile flow, which is directly related to radius

choiceNotes.b: Viscous loss alone keeps falling as the radius grows; the optimum is where the **total** of viscous and inertial energy is lowest.
choiceNotes.c: Inertial energy rises with radius; minimizing it alone ignores viscous loss. The optimum balances **both**.
